items.title: Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
items.summary: The culture secretary confirms reports they could be in the list of platforms set to be banned next March.
items.body: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said. Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe". The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.

items.title: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints
items.summary: MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to “It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is…
items.body: “I t started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence. “Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.” At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required.

items.title: How Dong Mingzhu, China’s manufacturing ‘iron lady’, is maintaining her cool in the AI era
items.summary: Dong Mingzhu chairs Gree Electric Appliances, a home-appliance giant based in southern China’s Guangdong province. Having worked her way up from a frontline sales job, she is one of China’s best-known figures in manufacturing. As a deputy to the National People’s Congress, she…
items.body: Dong Mingzhu chairs Gree Electric Appliances, a home-appliance giant based in southern China’s Guangdong province. Having worked her way up from a frontline sales job, she is one of China’s best-known figures in manufacturing. As a deputy to the National People’s Congress, she has long advocated for manufacturing innovation, higher incomes and greener consumption. In this interview, conducted when she was named an inaugural “Cool Leader” at an assembly of the UN Environment Programme’s Cool Coalition in Singapore, Dong discusses Chinese companies’ overseas expansion, how automation transforms manufacturing and her management philosophy. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. This summer, Chinese-made air conditioners helped Europeans cope with unprecedented heat.

items.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
items.summary: Parent company Pop Mart's revenue has fallen as appetite for the quirky collectible monsters wanes.
items.body: Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more. Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market. The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases. Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say". He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events. But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled.

items.title: 1-0 to humankind? US midterms vote puts AI, datacentres and the broligarchy back in their box | Heather Stewart
items.summary: Election results appear to have turbo-charged an already growing social, political and financial market rethink about AI ‘AI clog’: UK battles onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints Editorial: the AI backlash – Silicon Valley’s political power is cracking Last week’s midterms…
items.body: Last week’s midterms may not have cowed Donald Trump, but they should be a wake-up call for the grinning tech broligarchs who lined up at his inauguration two chaotic years ago. Clearly, the cost of living squeeze unleashed by Trump’s war in Iran was a big driver of the Democrat wave. But AI was also on the ballot – in many places, literally. Dozens of measures calling for limits on datacentre expansion were passed. And elsewhere, reining in the unchecked expansion of the power-hungry mega-sheds was a rallying cry. At a campaign event, the Texas senator-elect James Talarico recalled meeting a mother who told him the lights from the neighbouring datacentre were so bright, her son thought it was daytime in the middle of the night.

items.title: China urged to target sugar-rich drinks during consumption tax overhaul
items.summary: China has been urged to stop keeping beverage makers sweet and instead declare war on sugar-rich drinks through taxation, as the country moves to align its regulatory framework with global health promotion trends. A sugar tax has been proposed by experts and state media outlets,…
items.body: China has been urged to stop keeping beverage makers sweet and instead declare war on sugar-rich drinks through taxation, as the country moves to align its regulatory framework with global health promotion trends. A sugar tax has been proposed by experts and state media outlets, who argue that an ongoing overhaul of consumption taxes provides an ideal opportunity to wean consumers off the sweetener, which has been linked to increased risks of obesity and type 2 diabetes. People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s mouthpiece newspaper, has been among the voices calling for action, running articles in recent months discussing the pressing need for such a tax and practical steps towards its implementation. “A sugar tax is the prevailing trend,” it said in a report published in July.

items.title: Trump says renewed Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ if talks progress but warns he could still strike
items.summary: Trump tied avoiding renewed U.S. strikes to progress in talks over Iran’s nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.
items.body: President Donald Trump said he is "highly unlikely" to restart open war with Iran , but warned he could still strike the country as Washington tries to reach a deal with Tehran to end the conflict. The now more than eight-month-old war, which stoked inflation and sent oil prices surging, has seen repeated bursts of fighting separated by ceasefires and peace talks for months. It was widely speculated that Trump might restart open conflict after the midterm elections, where his Republican Party lost badly to Democrats. Trump's comments came during an interview with CNN , where he said restarting the war is unlikely as long as talks to constrain Iran's nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz make progress. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump said. "The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary.

items.title: Traders 'priced out' of £12,000 Christmas market pitches
items.summary: Stall holders said they'd met the council leader to express their concerns at high costs since a new operator took over.
items.body: They have told Liverpool City Council leader Liam Robinson that they cannot afford to take space at the event now that a new operator has taken over running it. Anthony Grice said he had been quoted £12,000 to take a stall at the St George's Plateau attraction. Robinson said he had met business owners to "understand the challenges and the issues that they might have had this year" so the authority could look at different options in future. He said the council had been aware of the price structure being offered to traders by the new operator, Underbelly, when it won the contract to run the event. But Grice said it felt like local traders' concerns were being "swept under the carpet" during a meeting to discuss the plans. He said: "I asked how many local traders had signed up, and the council didn't know".

items.title: UK spent £100m on zombie Brexit border inspection posts
items.summary: Five of seven facilities in England and Wales never reached operational stage as Tories vacillated over plans to check goods The UK wasted at least £100m in taxpayers’ money to set up zombie Brexit border inspection posts that were never used, it has been revealed. The overall…
items.body: The UK wasted at least £100m in taxpayers’ money to set up zombie Brexit border inspection posts that were never used, it has been revealed. The overall cost of Brexit was put at an estimated £4.7bn by the National Audit Office last year but this included years-long transformation of the software used for customs declarations and other systems built to cope with the UK leaving the single market. Now fresh information from HMRC on the exact spend on the seven “inland border facilities” has come to light. The sites were built but quickly decommissioned as the Conservative government at the time vacillated over plans to check goods coming in from the continent.

items.title: Robots’ arrival set to give Chinese asparagus farmers a boost
items.summary: In the flat, typhoon-prone fields of Lianshui county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, a once-obscure vegetable has become a local economic engine. Greenhouses for growing asparagus now cover more than 1,333 hectares (3,294 acres), produce 50,000 tonnes (55,116 short tons) a…
items.body: In the flat, typhoon-prone fields of Lianshui county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, a once-obscure vegetable has become a local economic engine. Greenhouses for growing asparagus now cover more than 1,333 hectares (3,294 acres), produce 50,000 tonnes (55,116 short tons) a year and generate over 1 billion yuan (US$150 million) in value, according to local government data. Lianshui accounts for about 30 per cent of China’s greenhouse-grown asparagus output, and much of the high-value white asparagus it produces ends up on plates in Japan, South Korea and Europe – markets where local production is expensive and shrinking. Once a rare foreign vegetable in China and still not a mainstay of Chinese cuisine, the “little spear” has led 2,300 farmers in the county to prosperity, with China now the world’s top supplier of processed asparagus after nearly three decades of rapid development.

items.title: Cathie Wood 'always feels better when the market is worried' — here's why
items.summary: The Ark Invest CEO said there was a "wall of worry" gripping markets right now.
items.body: Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood is shrugging off this week's market jitters, telling CNBC on Friday that concerns among investors actually reinforce her optimism that further gains lie ahead. U.S. equities sold off sharply on Thursday, reversing the initial rally seen in the wake of the midterm elections. AI-related stocks led the rout , sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory. On Friday, tech stocks staged a tentative recovery. Much of the sell-off on Thursday was driven by concerns that a Democrat-led Congress would lead to a slowdown in data center construction. But concerns about artificial intelligence – particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing – have sparked multiple bouts of volatility over the course of this year.

items.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
items.summary: The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls.
items.body: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather. "It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread." "I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further. "Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned. But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower. More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

items.title: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?
items.summary: As AI exposes flaws in IT systems and geopolitics plays out on the cyber frontline, some experts say the events of recent weeks could soon be a common occurrence Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week…
items.body: Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd. The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same. It was at this point that Pearce thought: is this a cyber-attack? He walked over to the box connecting the units to the internet and yanked out the cable. On the same day, retailers in Belgium , Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported similar problems, with refrigerators and freezers in some shops soaring to as high as 50C (122F). “If it had happened on a Saturday morning, when I don’t tend to be here, it could ultimately have led to a fire,” Pearce said. But it is not just Pearce and a disparate group of retailers, as well as French blood banks , that have been suffering.

items.title: How Democrats will try to end Trump's tariffs
items.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is likely the next House speaker, has made clear that ending President Trump's tariffs is one of Democrats' top priorities.
items.body: The battle for Congress is over. The war over President Donald Trump 's tariffs is about to heat up. The knotted web of tariffs that Trump spent the last two years weaving could soon face its biggest threat, as Democrats prepare to unload their new legislative firepower against the Republican president's signature policy. Democrats have made no secret of their plans to bombard Trump and his associates with investigations as soon as the next Congress is sworn in. They are also preparing a first-100-hours legislative blitz, putting forward a series of bills that would unwind much of Trump's agenda. Both prongs of attack will take aim at Trump's unprecedented use of tariffs , which Democrats have quickly identified as a main target following their landslide victory in Tuesday's midterm elections .

items.title: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
items.summary: Bailiffs reportedly seized digital records before court case over alleged intellectual property breaches on Land Rover Defender Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its…
items.body: Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its “Defender clone” infringes intellectual property rights. Bailiffs acting on behalf of JLR reportedly seized digital records from the offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp in August, according to the Sunday Times. The raid took place before a court case in the The Hague this week which will decide whether the BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender. Motoring experts have likened BYD’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year.

items.title: Democrats amp up Trump investigation threats, Blanche counters he may probe lawmakers
items.summary: Democrats have vowed to investigate both President Donald Trump's White House and businesses that have worked with the administration.
items.body: Top Democrats are ramping up oversight of the Trump administration and businesses it has partnered with, while Attorney General Todd Blanche warned he could counterinvestigate lawmakers conducting probes. Democrats romped to majorities in both the House and the Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, putting them in position to seize control of committee gavels and subpoena power in January. The electoral rout leaves Democrats with at least 54 Senate seats and 254 seats in the House of Representatives as votes continue to be counted in several states. Democrats vowed to investigate both President Donald Trump 's White House and businesses that have worked with the administration. CNBC reported on Thursday that Democrats are expected to take an aggressive approach to probing businesses, especially those companies with ties to the Trump family.

items.title: Amazon's Astro home robot has fans but looks destined for the 'trash heap.' Why it's trying again
items.summary: Amazon has formed a new home robotics team and is hiring for a “new-to-world robot product,” according to CNBC’s analysis of job posts.
items.body: Jeff Bezos made a bold bet in 2017. A sci-fi and robotics enthusiast, Bezos was convinced that consumers would have a robot in their home in the not-too-distant future. The Amazon founder and then-CEO told a group of the company's top device executives to get to work on building one, and within a few years, the team came up with the $1,450 Astro . The public got its first look at Astro, essentially an Alexa -equipped tablet on wheels that can autonomously navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, when it rolled on stage at Amazon's fall 2021 event. But it never evolved beyond an invite-only product. Astro shipped to just a few thousand customers, some of whom now believe the robot's days are numbered. The company also released an Astro for businesses in 2023, before sunsetting it less than a year later.

items.title: Banana producers in Latin America want better pay to cope with effects of climate crisis
items.summary: Farmers face big drop in production from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather…
items.body: Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event. High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic , farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions. Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador , and 6% in Peru compared with the year before.

items.title: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
items.summary: Thanksgiving airfare will cost more than last year as fares rise and strong demand continues.
items.body: Airline ticket prices have surged this year, especially for travel over the holidays. Don't expect many bargains if you're booking flights with miles, either. Tickets bought with frequent flyer miles for flights between large U.S. airports over the Thanksgiving travel period will cost 32% more than last year's holiday, according to data from Seats.aero, a miles and points redemption search site. While fares have skyrocketed this year, airline executives last month said demand remains strong. Airlines have largely gotten rid of static mileage redemption charts in favor of dynamic pricing, making budgeting for an award ticket more difficult. Dynamic pricing means redemption costs change depending on demand, routes and other factors.

items.title: ‘Free grand piano’: the scam playing on music lovers’ heartstrings
items.summary: Emails claim to come from a woman whose husband has died – but the offer isn’t what it seems An email pops up in your inbox: a woman whose husband has died is giving away his grand piano for free. She says she would love it to go to someone “who will truly appreciate and care…
items.body: A n email pops up in your inbox: a woman whose husband has died is giving away his grand piano for free. She says she would love it to go to someone “who will truly appreciate and care for it”. The piano “is in excellent condition and has brought joy to our home”. The email ends: “If you know of a dedicated student, teacher, family or church that would cherish this piano, please feel free to forward this message to them.” You don’t know the woman, but you are pretty sure your local school would love to have a grand piano. And if it doesn’t it, you’ll have it. The email address looks legitimate – it’s the woman’s name – so you reply and get into a dialogue about her late husband and the piano. Her story seems to stack up, and she says you sound ideal. The piano is in storage a couple of hundred miles away, she says, and you just need to pay for it to be delivered.

items.title: In pictures: France protests draw 146,000 as clashes erupt for fourth straight weekend
items.summary: France's Interior Ministry counted 146,000 protesters Saturday as demonstrations over living costs public services entered a fourth consecutive weekend.
items.body: Protesters clashed with police in France on Saturday as demonstrations over living costs and public services entered a fourth consecutive weekend and drew students, trade unions and members of the revived "Yellow Vest" movement onto the streets. The country's Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris. A youth union alliance put attendance at 250,000 nationally and 75,000 in the capital. At least 360 people were arrested across the country, AFP reported , citing a ministry tally. Police used tear gas against people throwing projectiles as the main Paris march ended at Place de la Nation, per AFP . Garbage cans were set alight as protesters and police clashed in several cities, according to Le Monde . Police blocked a separate, banned Yellow Vest gathering at Place de la Concorde and arrested two movement leaders, Le Monde reported.

items.title: US employers keep passing rising healthcare costs to workers. There are better options
items.summary: Choosing a healthcare plan can be extremely complicated, but it’s necessary to attract and retain good workers Again, healthcare costs are going up. According to a recent study from Mercer, total health benefit cost per employee in 2027 is expected to rise 8.2% – after…
items.body: A gain, healthcare costs are going up. According to a recent study from Mercer, total health benefit cost per employee in 2027 is expected to rise 8.2% – after employers’ planned cost-reduction measures (without action, employers told Mercer their existing plans would rise about 11%). This would be the highest increase since 2003. And, again, we see the same reaction from employers. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that even as healthcare costs have gone up, the share of these costs coming out employees’ paychecks has “shot up” even faster. Healthcare costs always rise. Naturally, employers are concerned about their bottom line. But is the right approach to pass these cost increases to employees? Or perhaps this is just a little shortsighted, if not lazy.

items.title: 'What makes you tick': NWSL, WNBA owner Kara Nortman on a personality test she uses to build success
items.summary: Kara Nortman, a top investor in women's pro sports teams, credits the Enneagram personality system for her own leadership instincts and team-building success.
items.body: Business leaders often look back to "aha" moments in their lives for enduring lessons about their success. For Kara Nortman, who had a long and successful career in technology and venture capital before becoming a women's professional sports owner, that moment arrived when she attended the 2015 Women's World Cup Final in Vancouver. After watching the U.S. team win, Nortman couldn't find a jersey to buy, or much of any merch, or even information online about women's soccer. And that gap stayed with her as something that suggested an untapped business opportunity. She began researching women's soccer, went on to advise the U.S. women's national team players' union, and ultimately co-founded Angel City Football Club in Los Angeles, the most valuable women's football club in the world, and now majority owned by former Disney CEO Bob Iger and his wife Willow Bay.

items.body: “My children started getting sick,” says Lois Bower-Bjornson, a campaigner at the Clean Air Council in Washington County, Pennsylvania. “My oldest son had rashes all over his body. His ears, his eyelids, everywhere. My youngest had terrible nosebleeds, it was so bad that he became anaemic and would almost pass out. He would wake up bleeding.” Bower-Bjornson blames her children’s health problems on the 36 fracking wells that surround her property in the greater Appalachian region of the US. She also places some of the responsibility on Ineos, a British company privately owned by British billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe , the co-owner of Premier League football club Manchester United.

items.title: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White press secretary job
items.summary: President Donald Trump offered the job of press secretary to UFC president and CEO Dana White on Saturday.
items.body: President Donald Trump offered UFC president and CEO Dana White the job of press secretary on Saturday. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said: "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States." "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote. "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Earlier Saturday, White posted a picture of himself on Instagram stories standing behind the press secretary's lectern in the White House, with the caption, "On to the next chapter." It was unclear whether White had accepted the position or was simply acknowledging the president's request as a joke.

items.title: What the Democratic sweep means for Trump's tariffs and AI
items.body: WASHINGTON/NEW YORK -- Democrats swept the U.S. midterm elections, winning control of both the House and Senate after voters delivered a major setback to President Donald Trump's Republican Party. Now attention is turning to what that shift could mean for Trump's economic agenda. A Democratic-controlled Congress could bring greater scrutiny of tariffs and trade deals, while voter opposition to data center development could slow the expansion of AI infrastructure in the U.S. Nikkei Asia's U.S. correspondents break down the election results and what comes next for tariffs, trade, agriculture and AI, as well as the potential repercussions for Asian economies and companies.

items.title: Indonesia's art deco hot spot, a century on
items.body: BANDUNG, Indonesia -- Bandung, the so-called Paris of Java, lies about 150 kilometers east of Jakarta, a distance that translates to a dizzying 30-minute ride on Indonesia's first high-speed rail link, plus a 10-minute journey to the city center on a local train. At over 750 meters above sea level, the city feels almost balmy compared with the stodgy heat of the capital.
